title: 1000 Layer Networks for Self-Supervised RL: Scaling Depth Can Enable New G

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states: 'Note additionally that the parameter count scales linearly with width but quadratically with depth.' This is mathematically incorrect for the described MLP architectures: with a fixed hidden unit width, the number of parameters scales quadratically with width (W^2 per layer) and linearly with depth (number of layers). The statement reverses the actual scaling relationship.

The abstract claims: 'Increasing model depth improves success rates modestly and occasionally corresponds to emergent behaviors in some humanoid tasks.' In contrast, the results section reports massive improvements (e.g., 20×, 42×, 50×, 600×) on locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks. Calling gains of 20–600× 'modest' grossly understates the findings and contradicts the experimental evidence presented in the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 16 (ablation on layer norm and Swish vs. ReLU)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 16 shows ablation results with a y-axis 'Time at Goal (0–700)' and a 'With Layer Norm' bar for depth 4 reaching around 600. In the main experimental results (Table 1 and Figure 1), the depth-4 CRL model with the same architectural components (including layer norm) achieves at most ~12.6 (Humanoid) or 308 (Arm Push Easy) Time at Goal. The figure does not specify the environment, but no reported environment attains ~600 at depth 4 under the same metric. This discrepancy renders the ablation results irreconcilable with the main findings.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.4, 'Deep Networks Unlock Batch Size Scaling'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The opening sentences claim that deeper networks can 'effectively leverage batch size scaling to achieve further improvements' and that 'larger networks can effectively leverage batch size scaling.' However, in the same paragraph the authors state: 'Figure 7 shows only marginal or inconsistent improvements from increasing batch size, even for larger depth models' and 'the overall benefit of batch size scaling remains uncertain and requires further investigation.' The initial strong positive claim is unsupported by their own evidence and is effectively retracted within the paragraph.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.4, 'Scaling the Actor vs. Critic Networks'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text asserts: 'with one environment (Ant Big Maze) demonstrating actor scaling to be more impactful.' The accompanying Figure 6 matrix for Ant Big Maze shows that increasing critic depth from 4 to 64 (while keeping actor depth fixed at 4) raises performance from 61 to 462, while increasing actor depth from 4 to 64 with critic depth 4 only raises performance from 61 to 72. Critic scaling produces a dramatically larger improvement, contradicting the claim that actor scaling is more impactful in this environment.
